1.text: ANIMAL FOOD. — The staple food of the Reindeer Chukchee is reindeer-

2.text: meat, and that of the Maritime people, “sea-meat,” — the meat of sea-mam-
2.note: Closing quote after "sea-meat," keyed curly (U+201D) per keying_spec.md §1/§5.6: "Quotation marks curly, never straight." Confirmed on sheet.

3.text: mals. On the whole, the latter is more relished by the whole people, because

4.text: it is fatter, and because it formed the chief food of their forefathers. The

5.text: reindeer-breeders have quite a liking for sea-food. This peculiarity may also

6.text: be observed in the traditions of the tribe. In the tale of Elendi and his

7.text: sons the old man and his wife risk the safety of their herd in sending their

8.text: sons to procure some sea-food. After a while, when the enemies have been

9.text: defeated, the old man is described as sitting in the sleeping-room, eating

10.text: blubber, the oil dripping down from both sides of his mouth. ¹
10.note: Footnote marker keyed as superscript U+00B9 per §2.10, matching the opener at line 38 (footnote 1).

11.text: I myself witnessed that Reindeer Chukchee who had not had any blubber

12.text: for a long time develop a craving for it, and are ready to pay extravagant

13.text: prices for it. For this reason every spring, when the traders from the sea-

14.text: coast visit the Reindeer camps, a continual feasting begins, and blubber and

15.text: meat of sea-animals are offered to every one as the best of dainties.

16.text: On the other hand, the Maritime Chukchee and the Eskimo value rein-

17.text: deer-meat very highly, and call it the “sweet food of reindeer-breeders.” In
17.note: Closing quote keyed curly (U+201D) per §1/§5.6, confirmed on sheet.

18.text: their tales it is often praised beyond any other kind of human food. The

19.text: Maritime people undertake long expeditions by sea and land to obtain a

20.text: supply, and occasionally trade some of it to the Eskimo of St. Lawrence

21.text: Island and of the Diomede Islands. Although the meat is usually in a very

22.text: poor state, it brings quite a good price. Generally it is bartered for the

23.text: meat of sea-mammals, because one of the principles of trade in those coun-

24.text: tries is the interchange of similar articles whenever possible. Cotton is traded

25.text: for skins, sugar for reindeer-tongues, ready-made shirts for ready-made skin

27.text: The Reindeer Chukchee have no opportunity to consume fish in any

28.text: considerable quantity. The Russianized natives, on the other hand, live almost

29.text: solely on fish; and therefore the Chukchee who live near these settlements

30.text: utilize fish, which they reckon as belonging to what is called “alien food.” ²
30.note: Closing quote keyed curly (U+201D, §1/§5.6); footnote marker keyed as superscript U+00B2 per §2.10, matching the opener at line 37 (footnote 2). Confirmed on sheet.

31.text: The Maritime Chukchee also consider fish as rather poor diet. ³ They con-
31.note: Footnote marker keyed as superscript U+00B3 per §2.10, matching the opener at line 36 (footnote 3).

32.text: sume it, however, whenever they have a chance to obtain it, and also gather

33.text: oysters and shells on sandy beaches or in shallow waters.

34.text: METHODS OF COOKING. — At present most of the meat is eaten boiled.
34.note: mz/ocr machine draft read "COORING"; the printed word is "COOKING", confirmed at 2x zoom (review/1-249/zoom/zoom2-34p1-73.png). CATMuS is not a witness to letter identity (this guidance applies generally, not only to Tier-1 glyphs).
